newsitem.title: USA: Xerox unveils digital copier family.
newsitem.headline: Xerox unveils digital copier family.

text.p: Xerox Corp said it introduced a family of digital copier products that can be upgraded from stand-alone copiers to a device that is part of an office network, capable of printing, faxing and scanning.

Xerox on Tuesday unveiled the Document Centre 220 and 230 with optional facsimile capability. These units are available now, with networked versions available in the fourth quarter. The other two models, the Document Centre 240 and 265 will be available in the second half of 1997.
Xerox CEO Paul Allaire said he expects revenues for the new products to reach $2 billion "over time."

Allaire said at a press conference that he expects the new digital products to be more successful than Xerox's DocuTech high speed copier family, which it introduced in 1990. It had about $1.8 billion in revenues last year.

"We expect it to be more important than DocuTech," Allaire said, adding that it took about six years for the DocuTech to reach its current revenue stream. "That gives you an idea," he told Reuters, when asked about how long it will take the new digital copiers to reach $2 billion in revenues.
Xerox also plans to roll out color digital copiers in a few weeks, as part of its vision of a "digital future."
"Digital is growing in excess of 20 percent every year," Allaire said, adding that sales of digital products will become an increasingly bigger part of its overall revenues.
In 1996, Xerox said sales of its digital products were over 30 percent of its total 1996 revenues of $17.4 billion.
"Every year it will be bigger," Allaire said.

Allaire and other Xerox executives said one of the features of the new products that is appealing to its customers is that they can either act as a stand-alone copier or they can be upgraded, in stages, to become a part of a corporate computer network.

Xerox has invested over $500 million over a period of years in the development of this next generation architecture, but Allaire emphasized that it will not abandon its analog copiers, which cannot be hooked up to digital devices.

"There are some instances where a light lens copier still makes sense," Allaire said, adding that Xerox has already introduced five analog copiers earlier this year and more launches are expected this year.
"Our intention is to grow our market share in the light lens area," Allaire said, referring to conventional copiers. Over half of Xerox's revenues still come from analog copiers.
"But make no mistake, the future does belong to digital," Allaire told the press conference.

The first two products available, the 220 and the 230 Digital Copiers produce images with laser clarity at 400 by 400 dots per inch in copier and fax mode. When they are used as printers, the resolution is even higher at 600 by 600 dots per inch. The devices scan and copy at speeds of 20 and 30 pages respectively. The 220 is priced at $8,600 for the basic model and the 230 lists for $10,500 in the U.S.
The other two models, the 240 and the 265 Digital Copiers, will be priced when they are available in the second half.
